intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, tells you what to remember and warns where communicators slip. Work the section exercises in pencil, check yourself with the recall questions, and keep the law pages open with the date they were checked beside them.

sections.title: Why media matters for development work
sections.big_idea: Evidence changes nothing until it reaches the people who decide. Plan **the journey to the decision** from the first day of the study.
in_plain_words: Development organisations produce surveys, evaluations and briefs that few people read. The decisions they should inform are taken by officials, legislators, funders, journalists and families who will never open the PDF. Media are the channels that carry evidence to them. Separate the four jobs communication does: inform the public, influence policy, change behaviour, and account and be accountable. Each has its own audience, channel and test of success.

Choose by influence as well as reach. A district collector may skip the prime-time debate and read a two-paragraph item in the local Hindi daily. Know how connected your audience is, mix paid, earned, shared and owned channels, and plan for criticism as well as launches. **Write down the decision you want to change** before you list the outlets.

key_terms.meaning: Paid, earned, shared and owned media: four channel groups with different control and credibility.
How many people a message touches.
Whether the people who control a decision take the message seriously.
Coverage an editor chooses to give, such as news items and op-eds.
Your own website, reports, newsletter and podcast.
Answering queries, corrections and crises under deadline.

worked_example.title: Who does a smartphone-only plan miss?
worked_example.setup: You plan a campaign for women aged 15-49 that depends on internet use. The deck gives NFHS-6 figures (provisional).
steps: Women who have ever used the internet: 64.3%. Those who have not: 100 − 64.3 = 35.7.
Women with a phone they use themselves: 63.6%. Those without: 100 − 63.6 = 36.4.
Rural women who have ever used the internet: 58.6%. Those who have not: 100 − 58.6 = 41.4.
So a digital-only plan misses roughly a third of women, and more in rural districts.
Add a channel they use: radio, frontline workers or printed material.
worked_example.answer: About 36 per cent of women are missed overall and about 41 per cent of rural women, so a non-internet channel is needed.

mistakes: Mixing the four jobs together, so a plan produces activity with no visible change.
Judging success by the outlets you reached instead of the decision you wanted to change.
Budgeting only for proactive launches and meeting a hostile query or a crisis unprepared.
Assuming the biggest audience decides. A local-edition item may matter more than prime time.

recall.q: Name the four jobs communication does in a programme.
recall.a: Inform the public, influence policy, change behaviour, and account and be accountable.

recall.q: What do the letters in PESO stand for?
recall.a: Paid, earned, shared and owned media.

recall.q: Which type of media has full control but credibility that depends on your reputation?
recall.a: Owned media.

recall.q: What share of women aged 15-49 have ever used the internet, per NFHS-6?
recall.a: 64.3%, provisional.

recall.q: What should you write down before the outlets you want to be in?
recall.a: The decision or behaviour you want to change.

sections.title: How the media market works in South Asia
sections.big_idea: India's media are **many language markets, regionally concentrated and dependent on advertising**. Choose outlets by audience, owner and language.
in_plain_words: No single regulator covers Indian media. Print, cable, radio, telecom and online each sit under a different law and body. The Media Ownership Monitor found ownership plural nationally but concentrated in regional language markets, where a few papers reach most readers. Advertising, much of it from governments, funds most outlets, which can shape what gets covered.

Language is the practical lever. Hindi is the largest at 43.63%, but a large public reads other languages, and English reaches a small, influential slice. Budget for translation and a spokesperson in each language, and release translations the same day. In the region, risks differ by country, so **ask local partners what the law allows** before putting a name to a quote.

children.label: Print and press ethics
items: Press and Registration of Periodicals Act 2023

diagram.caption: different media, different laws and bodies

key_terms.meaning: Press Registrar General of India, for newspapers and periodicals.
Press Council of India, the statutory body on press ethics.
RSF and DataLEADS study of ownership at 58 leading outlets.
A few owners holding most of the readership in a market.
The Constitution's list of 22 recognised languages.
Revenue mainly from adverts, with governments the main source.

worked_example.title: How much does English-only miss?
worked_example.setup: Census 2011 gives the share of the population returning each of the seven largest scheduled languages as mother tongue.
worked_example.answer: These seven languages together are 79.69% of the population, and English reaches a small slice, so budget for translation.

mistakes: Judging a launch by two or three English national dailies.
Offering paid placement or 'advertorial' in exchange for coverage.
Treating the internet subscription count as the number of people online.
Using one press strategy across the region without asking local partners about their law.

recall.q: Which body governs press ethics in India?
recall.a: The Press Council of India, under the Press Council Act 1978.

recall.q: What did the Media Ownership Monitor find about regional markets?
recall.a: Ownership looks plural nationally but is highly concentrated in regional language markets.

recall.q: What share of Hindi print readership did four outlets hold?
recall.a: 76.45% of the national Hindi market.

recall.q: Why can heavy state advertising matter to your launch?
recall.a: A study critical of a state scheme may be harder to place, so brief several outlets and publish the full study on your own site.

recall.q: What does the deck advise about translations at a launch?
recall.a: Release them the same day as the English version.

sections.title: Broadcast, radio and community media
sections.big_idea: Akashvani, DD FreeDish and community radio **reach people the internet still misses**, but each tier has its own rule on news.
in_plain_words: Radio has three tiers. Public service radio (Akashvani) covers 98% of the population and alone may originate news. Private FM may broadcast music and entertainment but not its own news. Community radio is built for local voice, with a 5-10 km range, 50% locally generated content, capped advertising, and only Akashvani news.

Work with community stations on their terms: offer content their community wants, bring local speakers, respect editorial control and pay production costs. SITE and Kheda show the shift from broadcasting to people towards producing with people. Television is changing too: pay DTH subscribers fell, and free satellite and DD FreeDish reach households that neither pay nor use much mobile data. **Name the source and date of every figure**, as two official counts of community stations differ.

diagram.caption: three tiers of radio with different news rules

key_terms.meaning: Runs Akashvani (radio) and Doordarshan (television).
A free-to-air satellite service with no monthly subscription.
A non-profit local station with limited advertising and no own news.
The 1975-76 satellite television experiment reaching about 2,400 villages.
A field laboratory for locale-specific programming in one district.
Paid direct-to-home satellite television.

worked_example.title: Community radio limits for a series
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A station is on air 14 hours a day and you plan a paid-for series on entitlements.
steps: Advertising cap is 12 minutes per hour of broadcast: 12 × 14 = 168 minutes a day.
Convert to hours: 168 ÷ 60 = 2.8 hours.
Local content must be at least 50%: 14 × 0.5 = 7 hours a day.
A story about your study counts as news and current affairs, so it must come from Akashvani.
Offer a drama, phone-in or local talk show instead.
worked_example.answer: No more than 168 minutes of advertising and at least 7 hours of local content a day; the news item itself is not allowed.

mistakes: Expecting a private FM station to carry a news story about your study.
Sending a press release to a community station and expecting it to be read out.
Asking a community station to carry political messaging.
Quoting a station count without its source and date when two official counts differ.

recall.q: Who may originate radio news in India?
recall.a: Only the public broadcaster, Akashvani.

recall.q: What share of content must community radio generate with community participation?
recall.a: At least 50%.

recall.q: What is the advertising cap on community radio?
recall.a: 12 minutes per hour of broadcast.

recall.q: What did SITE test?
recall.a: Whether centrally produced television could carry messages on agriculture, health and family planning to rural audiences at scale.

recall.q: How many community radio stations did PIB and TRAI count in 2026?
recall.a: 528 (PIB, February) and 564 operational (TRAI, 31 March).

sections.title: Platforms, messaging apps and misinformation
sections.big_idea: On messaging apps **a correction must travel the same chain as the claim**. Make the true version short, local and forwardable.
in_plain_words: Online news is led by video platforms and messaging apps, but the Reuters sample is mostly English-speaking and online. Trust in news in India is 39%, so a low-trust outlet may persuade few people outside its audience. On messaging apps, trust attaches to the person who forwarded the message, so public corrections never reach the groups where a claim travelled.

The LSE study found that prejudice and ideology drove sharing more than digital illiteracy, and sharing followed caste, religion and gender. Respond with the four steps of detect, assess, respond and follow up, using a trusted local voice. Plan for shutdowns as well: keep an offline route for every critical message.

left.title: Public platform
items: Trust comes from brand and account

right.title: Messaging app
items: Trust comes from who forwarded it
Correction must travel the same chain

key_terms.meaning: Reuters Institute's annual survey of online news users.
A private or group chat, often end-to-end encrypted.
A short, local-language, sourced item that is easy to pass on.
Teaching that draws on constitutional values and human rights.
Deliberate switching off of internet access, often in a district.
Access Now's coalition that counts shutdowns.

worked_example.title: Two numbers to quote with care
worked_example.setup: The 2026 Digital News Report puts trust in news in India at 39%, a fall of four percentage points. #KeepItOn counted 313 shutdowns in 2025, 195 of them in Asia-Pacific countries.
steps: Previous year's trust: 39 + 4 = 43%, so the change is a fall of four points.
Share of recorded shutdowns in Asia-Pacific: 195 ÷ 313 = 0.62.
So about 62% of the recorded shutdowns were in 11 Asia-Pacific countries.
Quote the source, the year and 'at least', since 313 is a minimum count.
worked_example.answer: Trust was 43% the year before; about 62% of recorded shutdowns were in Asia-Pacific.

mistakes: Assuming people forward false messages because they cannot tell true from false.
Arguing with individuals in large groups, or mocking people who believed the claim.
Repeating the false claim in the headline or image of your correction.
Issuing a long denial in English when the rumour is circulating in Bhojpuri.

recall.q: What did the Reuters India sample mainly represent?
recall.a: Urban, connected, English-using audiences.

recall.q: What is overall trust in news in India in the 2026 report?
recall.a: 39%, eighteenth of 48 markets.

recall.q: What did the LSE study find drove WhatsApp sharing?
recall.a: Prejudice and ideology, more than digital illiteracy.

recall.q: What are the four steps for responding to misinformation?
recall.a: Detect, assess, respond and follow up.

recall.q: What should you keep for every critical message?
recall.a: An offline route, such as radio, printed material or frontline workers.

sections.title: Press freedom and the Constitution
sections.big_idea: The press is free because **speech is free under Article 19(1)(a)**, limited only on the eight grounds in Article 19(2).
in_plain_words: India has no separate press clause. The Supreme Court read press freedom into Article 19(1)(a), and Article 19(2) permits reasonable restrictions on eight grounds. A restriction must fall within a ground, link closely to it and be proportionate. Romesh Thappar, Shreya Singhal and Anuradha Bhasin show courts applying these tests.

Defamation is still a crime, under BNS s356, so a complaint can be filed in a court far from your office. Journalists also face danger, which gives you a duty of care to sources and partners. RSF ranks India 157th of 180, but a few points of score can move many places, so **cite the indicator and method with any rank**.

events.what: Romesh Thappar: press ban struck down

diagram.caption: five dates for Article 19 in practice

key_terms.meaning: The right to freedom of speech and expression.
Lists the grounds for reasonable restrictions on speech.
The test that a restriction be closely linked and not excessive.
IT Act provision on offensive messages, struck down in 2015.
The criminal defamation offence in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023.
RSF's World Press Freedom Index of 180 countries.

worked_example.title: Read RSF's change for India
worked_example.setup: RSF gives India rank 157 and score 31.96 in 2026, and rank 151 and score 32.96 in 2025.
steps: Change in rank: 157 − 151 = 6 places lower.
Change in score: 32.96 − 31.96 = 1 point lower.
Category: below 40 is 'very serious', so India stays in that band both years.
Caution: a few points of score can move a country many places, so quote the score and method.
worked_example.answer: India fell six places on a one-point drop in score and stays in the 'very serious' band.

mistakes: Quoting a rank without the edition, indicator and method.
Assuming criminal defamation has gone because it was challenged. It survived in 2016.
Naming a source or village in a story without their informed agreement.
Relying on a restriction that does not fall within one of the eight grounds.

recall.q: Where does India's constitutional protection for the press sit?
recall.a: In Article 19(1)(a), the right to speech and expression, as read by the Supreme Court.

recall.q: How many grounds does Article 19(2) list?
recall.a: Eight.

recall.q: What did Shreya Singhal strike down?
recall.a: Section 66A of the IT Act, in its entirety.

recall.q: What did Anuradha Bhasin direct about shutdown orders?
recall.a: They must be published, temporary, proportionate and open to review.

recall.q: What is India's 2026 rank in RSF's index?
recall.a: 157 of 180, down six places.

sections.title: The legal frame for communicators
sections.big_idea: Most communicators fall into **eight well-known legal traps**. Run sensitive material through the risk table before it goes out.
in_plain_words: Defamation (BNS s356) covers companies as well as people, and the defences depend on truth for the public good, fair opinion on public conduct, accurate court reports and good faith. Keep notes and drafts and print the reply of anyone criticised. The IT Rules, the programme code for cable and the Press Council norms add rules for particular media, and some rules have been stayed or struck down.

Other traps are the election period (RP Act), copyright, contempt of court, identifying a rape or child victim, and personal data. The DPDP Act duties start on 13 May 2027, but consent and records should begin now. **Check the current status of any provision** before you rely on it.

key_terms.meaning: An imputation intended or likely to harm a person's reputation.
Publishing the response of a person or body criticised.
Content rules for anything transmitted on cable under the 1995 Act.
Quoting for review, criticism or reporting current events.
Commenting on pending cases in a way that prejudges them.
Personal data law with duties starting 13 May 2027.

worked_example.title: Screen a draft case study
worked_example.setup: A draft names a contractor as responsible for broken toilets, uses a photograph from a stringer, and names the village of a girl who missed school.
steps: Naming the contractor is defamation risk (BNS s356): keep evidence, ask for a response and print it.
The stringer's photograph is not commissioned or licensed: seek a licence or stay within fair dealing.
A named village plus a girl may identify a child: JJ Act s74 and POCSO s23 say stop and remove the identity.
Check for a polling area or a pending case in the same period.
worked_example.answer: Revise before publishing: evidence and reply for the contractor, a licence for the photograph and no identifying detail for the girl.

mistakes: Describing the offence as gone because the IPC sections were replaced. BNS s356 carries it.
Treating a public service spot as outside the cable programme code.
Relying on a rule that a court has stayed without checking its current status.
Waiting for the DPDP duties before recording consent.

recall.q: Can a company be defamed under the BNS?
recall.a: Yes, Explanation 2 covers a company or an association.

recall.q: Which exceptions matter most to development communicators?
recall.a: Truth for public good, good faith opinion on public conduct (two exceptions), court reports and protection of interests.

recall.q: What does the PCI's Norm 41 require?
recall.a: Publishing the reply of a person or body criticised.

recall.q: Who owns a commissioned photograph unless the contract says otherwise?
recall.a: The person who commissioned it for valuable consideration.

recall.q: When do the DPDP duties and penalties start?

sections.title: Communication for development: theory and critique
sections.big_idea: Development communication moved from **telling people** to **producing with people**. Know which model your project actually uses.
in_plain_words: The modernisation model, from Lerner and Schramm, assumed information flowed from experts to the public and more media meant new attitudes and behaviour. Rogers's diffusion model added how practices spread through neighbours and trusted adopters. Rogers himself then listed the criticisms: top-down, deficit view, blind to structure, pro-innovation bias and media-centric.

Freire contrasted banking education with dialogue, and participatory communication puts production in community hands. Today's four families are behaviour change, media advocacy, research communication and community media. Participation can fail, so apply the test: **could the people consulted change the plan?** If not, call it consultation.

key_terms.meaning: Communication for development: planned use of communication to support change.
How a new practice spreads through a social system.
Experts deposit a message into passive audiences.
Communities define the problem and communication changes both sides.
Treating poor people as lacking information when they lacked resources or power.
Community-produced media as a form of participation.

worked_example.title: Place four statements on the map
worked_example.setup: A funder's brief makes four statements about a radio campaign. Which model does each reflect?
steps: 'More exposure will change attitudes, then behaviour.' This is the modernisation model.
'Farmers copy a neighbour who tried the seed.' This is diffusion, with trusted local adopters.
'Success means the audience repeats the message.' This is the banking model.
'Success means communities act on their own analysis, even against us.' This is the dialogic model.
Decide which of these your own plan relies on.
worked_example.answer: Modernisation, diffusion, banking, dialogic. Most real programmes combine more than one.

mistakes: Counting exposure as success, whatever happened afterwards.
Blaming 'laggards' for structural barriers such as land, credit, time or power.
Reporting three selected quotations as 'community voice'.
Promising behaviour change from what is really a media relations exercise.

recall.q: Which two books defined the modernisation approach?
recall.a: Lerner's The Passing of Traditional Society and Schramm's Mass Media and National Development.

recall.q: What did Rogers's 1976 article describe?
recall.a: The dominant model, the factors behind its decline and the emerging alternatives.

recall.q: What is the 'banking' model?
recall.a: Teaching, or communication, in which experts deposit knowledge into passive students or audiences.

recall.q: Name two warning signs of poor participation.
recall.a: Any two of: the same few speak, women and Dalit and Adivasi members appear only in photographs, content never criticises the programme, decisions were taken first.

recall.q: What is the test of participation?
recall.a: Whether the people consulted could change the plan.

sections.title: Writing for different audiences
sections.big_idea: One finding needs **several documents**, each written for a different reader, with the finding first and every number checkable.
in_plain_words: Write the full report first, then the brief, then the release, and link each shorter document to the longer one. A press release uses the inverted pyramid, with the finding in the headline and a named contact. An op-ed makes one argument with sourced evidence and a counter-argument. An explainer follows the reader's questions in order, without arguing a position.

Data stories need the level, the change, the comparison group and the survey round. Say 'percentage points' for differences between percentages. Write in plain language, name the people and bodies, and give the numbers. **Every number in a release must be true and checkable**, and each one needs a source.

key_terms.meaning: Most important fact first, then detail, then background.
A signed argument on a newspaper's opinion page.
A piece built from the reader's questions, without taking a position.
The unit for the difference between two percentages.
The population a percentage is calculated from.
Naming people, bodies and numbers instead of insider terms.

worked_example.title: Describe the NFHS-6 change accurately
worked_example.setup: Women aged 15-49 who have ever used the internet: 33.3% in NFHS-5 and 64.3% in NFHS-6 (provisional). Illustrative survey in a release: 41% of 1,200 girls missed school.
steps: Change in points: 64.3 − 33.3 = 31 percentage points.
Relative rise: 64.3 ÷ 33.3 = 1.93, which is a 93% rise. Quoted alone it hides the level.
Write: almost two in three women, up from one in three, a rise of 31 percentage points.
In the release example, count the girls: 1,200 × 0.41 = 492.
Give the base and the place: 492 of 1,200 girls in four Bihar blocks.
worked_example.answer: Use '31 percentage points' with the level and comparison, and give the base for every percentage.

mistakes: Reporting a percentage without its base, or confusing percentages and percentage points.
A headline that names the organisation and not the finding.
Using terms such as capacity building and convergence that mean nothing to a reader.
Presenting a provisional figure as final.

recall.q: In what order should the written products be written?
recall.a: The full report first, then the brief, then the release.

recall.q: What goes in a press release headline?
recall.a: The finding, with a number, in plain words.

recall.q: What structure does the deck suggest for an op-ed?
recall.a: Hook, argument, evidence, counter-argument and close.

recall.q: What does a data story need beyond the number?
recall.a: The level, the change, the comparison group and the survey round.

recall.q: How should Rs 2,50,00,000 be written for readers?
recall.a: Rs 2.5 crore.

sections.title: Working with journalists and platforms
sections.big_idea: Journalists need **a news angle, checkable data and a spokesperson on the day**. Build the relationship before you need it.
in_plain_words: A story passes reporters, desks, editors and often stringers, under tight deadlines. Editors judge by six news values: novelty, impact, proximity, timeliness, conflict and human interest. Lead with district figures for a regional paper. Give interviews on the record unless you agree other terms in advance, and prepare three messages with a fact each.

Use an embargo when it buys better coverage, and remember that it rests on trust. Correct errors by following the four-step ladder, and correct your own faster. Treat organisational social media as a publishing channel with an editor, a policy and a log, and share well-documented data with journalists. **Never share data that could identify a respondent.**

key_terms.meaning: Criteria editors use to choose stories, such as novelty and impact.
An agreement not to publish before a stated date and time.
Quotable with your name and role.
Usable but attributed to a description, such as a researcher involved.
Not to be published or attributed; binds only if agreed beforehand.
A district reporter often paid per story.

worked_example.title: Date the embargo
worked_example.setup: Your embargo lifts at 00:01 IST on 14 March. Material goes to reporters 2 to 5 days ahead.
steps: Earliest send date: 14 − 5 = 9 March.
Latest send date: 14 − 2 = 12 March.
State the embargo with its time zone in the subject line and at the top of each document.
Offer briefings and interviews before 14 March.
Publish the report on your website at embargo time.
worked_example.answer: Send between 9 and 12 March, with the embargo written as 00:01 IST, 14 March.

mistakes: Calling at deadline to ask whether the reporter got the release.
Asking to see or approve the story before publication.
Threatening legal action over an honest mistake or demanding takedown.
Sending an embargoed study to journalists you do not trust, without a plan for it breaking.

recall.q: Name the six news values.
recall.a: Novelty, impact, proximity, timeliness, conflict and human interest.

recall.q: What is an embargo?
recall.a: An agreement that a journalist receives material in advance and does not publish before a stated date and time.

recall.q: Which interview term binds only if agreed beforehand?
recall.a: Off the record.

recall.q: What does the deck say to do if a story gets it wrong?
recall.a: Check, contact the reporter with the correction and evidence, write to the editor if unresolved, and for print complain to the Press Council.

recall.q: Which data should you never share with journalists?
recall.a: Individual-level data that could identify a respondent.

sections.title: Images, consent, crises and access
sections.big_idea: Dignity, consent and access are a **routine before every publication**, and a crisis plan is agreed before a crisis.
in_plain_words: Development imagery has long shown poor people as helpless. The Dóchas guide asks for authentic representation, contributor-led stories, informed consent and no harm. Informed consent is a process of explaining, asking, recording and respecting refusal. Children and survivors of sexual violence must never be identified, even remotely, and a dignity checklist catches most problems.

In a crisis, silence and defensiveness cause most damage. Use the six CERC principles and a first-24-hours playbook with a holding statement and one spokesperson. Accessible communication is a legal duty under the RPwD Act: captions, transcripts, sign language, alt text and language access. **When in doubt, do not publish, or use an illustration.**

diagram.caption: consent is a process, reviewed before reuse

key_terms.meaning: Agreement given after understanding who sees the image, where, how long and the risk.
Identifying someone through indirect details such as a village or uniform.
A short signed statement of what is known and when the next update comes.
The CDC's crisis communication principles: first, right, credible, empathy, action, respect.
A record linking each image to its consent.
Content available with captions, transcripts, sign language and alt text.

worked_example.title: Dignity-check a photograph
worked_example.setup: A photograph for a donor report shows a girl in school uniform outside a broken toilet, captioned 'beneficiary of our sanitation project'.
steps: Consent: is there a record for this specific use? If not, stop.
Identification: a school uniform and the school name could identify a child. Remove the identifying detail or use an illustration.
Caption: is she a beneficiary of something she did not receive? Correct the caption.
Dignity: would she be comfortable seeing this image with this caption?
If any stop question is answered yes, do not publish.
worked_example.answer: Do not publish as it stands. Obtain recorded consent, remove identifying detail and fix the caption, or use an illustration.

mistakes: Treating a quick 'photo le sakte hain?' as informed consent.
Blurring a face while leaving a named village or uniform that identifies a survivor.
Saying 'no comment' or blaming the people affected in a crisis.
Using a stock image as if it were your programme.

recall.q: Name the four Dóchas commitments.
recall.a: Authentic representation, contributor-led stories and locally led content, informed consent, and upholding standards and doing no harm.

recall.q: What are the four steps of consent?
recall.a: Explain, ask, record and respect.

recall.q: What does BNS s72 punish?
recall.a: Printing or publishing the name or identity of a victim of rape and related offences.

recall.q: What are the six CERC principles?
recall.a: Be first, be right, be credible, express empathy, promote action and show respect.

recall.q: What does RPwD Act s42 require of media content?
recall.a: Accessible format, including audio description, sign language interpretation and close captioning.

sections.title: Measuring and planning: a practitioner toolkit
sections.big_idea: Measure **what communication changed** as well as what it produced, and fill in a one-page plan months before release.
in_plain_words: AMEC's framework runs from objectives through inputs, activities, outputs, outtakes and outcomes to impact. Outputs are what was published, outtakes are audience response, outcomes are change in the audience and impact is the decision or practice change your programme exists for. Avoid advertising value equivalents, which price coverage as advertising.

Choose a few indicators at each stage and set them before launch. A one-page plan covers objective, audiences, messages, messengers, channels, timing, risks and measures. Before publishing, use the risk table and the checklist. **Accuracy of coverage is an indicator**, and impact is recorded as a contribution alongside other pressures.

levels.label: Objectives
levels.sub: what you set out to change

key_terms.meaning: What was published and where, such as articles and broadcast mentions.
The response and reactions of target audiences.
The effect of the communication on the target audience.
The effect on the organisation's objectives.
Advertising value equivalent: pricing coverage as if it were advertising.
Crediting a change to your work alongside other pressures.

worked_example.title: Score the accuracy of coverage
worked_example.setup: Illustrative worked example in the deck: coverage appeared in six Hindi and two English outlets, and five stated the finding accurately.
steps: Total outlets: 6 + 2 = 8.
Accuracy share: 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625, or 62.5%.
That is an output indicator: 'share of items stating the finding correctly'.
Pair it with outtakes (40 brief downloads from government addresses) and outcomes (officials who can state the finding).
worked_example.answer: 62.5% of the coverage was accurate, a figure to improve by corrections and briefings.

mistakes: Reporting only counts of releases and followers as results.
Collecting media monitoring alone and calling it evaluation.
Claiming sole credit for a policy change.
Leaving the plan until after the study, when it should be filled in at the start.

recall.q: What are outtakes in the AMEC framework?
recall.a: The response and reactions of target audiences.

recall.q: Which stage is the decision or practice change your programme exists for?
recall.a: Impact.

recall.q: Why avoid AVEs?
recall.a: They price coverage as if it were advertising, which says nothing about change.

recall.q: Name three headings of the one-page communication plan.
recall.a: Any three of: objective, audiences, messages, messengers, channels, timing, risks, measures.

recall.q: How did the worked example record the department's circular?
recall.a: As a contribution alongside other pressures, without claiming sole credit.

sections.title: Summing up and where next
sections.big_idea: Know the decision, know the audience, **check the law, tell it straight**, then measure what changed.
in_plain_words: The ten key ideas run from deciding what you want to change, through the market, radio, messaging apps, press freedom and defamation, to writing, journalists and measurement. Two are non-negotiable: never identify a survivor or a protected child, and recheck the law because rules move.

The related courses split into communication and evidence, and law, ethics and participation. The suggested order is Advocacy Basics, then Data Visualization, then Safeguarding & PSEA. Read the data protection course before 13 May 2027. **Use the ten ideas as your own audit** of a live project.

key_terms.meaning: Start from the decision or behaviour to change, then pick audiences and channels.
India's media as regional language markets dependent on advertising.
Eight grounds on which speech may be restricted.
The reply of anyone criticised, printed alongside.
Never identify a survivor or a protected child, even remotely.
The share of coverage stating your finding correctly.

worked_example.title: Pick your next course
worked_example.setup: You run a research team that will launch a district study next quarter and plans to tell survivors' stories.
steps: Start with Advocacy Basics for media advocacy within a wider campaign.
Next take Data Visualization for charts that survive a newspaper page.
Then Safeguarding & PSEA, which the deck says to read before telling any survivor's story.
Read Data Protection & the DPDP Act before 13 May 2027.
worked_example.answer: Advocacy Basics, Data Visualization, Safeguarding & PSEA, and the DPDP course before the duties begin.

mistakes: Treating the legal summary as legal advice for a specific publication.
Skipping the pre-publication checklist because the deadline is near.
Starting with outlets and ending with a decision nobody was targeting.
Relying on provisions without rechecking whether a court has stayed them.

recall.q: What is the first of the ten ideas?
recall.a: Start from the decision or behaviour you want to change, then choose audiences and channels.

recall.q: Which defences does the deck name for defamation?
recall.a: Truth for the public good and fair comment.

recall.q: Which three media reach people the internet still misses?
recall.a: Akashvani, DD FreeDish and community radio.

recall.q: What does the deck say about corrections?
recall.a: Treat journalists as professionals: news values, embargoes, clear terms and fast corrections.

recall.q: What is the deck's closing line?
recall.a: Know the decision, know the audience, check the law, tell it straight.

notes.2: Use the agenda as a map by job. Sections 2 to 4 describe the media you work in, 5 and 6 the law around it, 7 the theory, and 8 to 11 the practical craft. If you are planning a launch, read sections 8, 9 and 11 first and return to the law before you publish.
notes.4: Start with the journey the evidence must make. The decision-makers named here will never open your PDF, so the question is which channel carries your finding to them. **Plan that route on the first day of the study**, and use the coverage list to find the skill you need.
notes.5: Name which of the four jobs you are doing before you plan anything. Each has a different audience and a different test of success, and the slide says mixing them up is the commonest reason for activity without change. **Write one success line per job**, taken from the right-hand column.
notes.6: Plan for the traffic that runs back at you. The channels that carry your evidence will carry criticism of it, so budget time for reactive work as well as the launch. The slide's two examples are a photograph shared without consent and **an overstated pilot result**.
notes.7: Use these figures to check your channel before you choose it. Among women aged 15-49, 64.3% have used the internet and 63.6% have a phone they use themselves, with a clear rural gap. A smartphone-only plan **misses roughly a third of women**, so add radio or face-to-face routes.
notes.8: Reach is a count and influence is a person. Before naming outlets, answer the slide's questions about who takes the decision, what that person reads and when the decision is made. Then **write down the decision you want to change** before you list a single outlet.
notes.9: Memorise PESO and use it as a channel-mix test. Paid gives control but low credibility, earned gives credibility but low control, and most campaigns combine at least three types. The row to remember is shared media, where **control is very low once it travels**.
notes.10: Read this as a user manual for the whole deck. Most law and market data are Indian, with neighbours added where the risk changes. The law is stated as of October 2026, and two rules discussed here were stayed or struck down, so **check current status before relying on any provision**.
notes.12: Let the scale shape your plan. With thousands of outlets, mostly regional and in languages other than English, 'getting into the media' means choosing. Note the caveat under the figures: subscriptions count connections, so **1,092.79 million is larger than the number of people online**.
notes.13: Use the table to find the right regulator before you act. A communicator working across print, cable, radio and online meets several bodies, each under a different law. Circle the row that matches your format and note its Act, since **no single regulator covers Indian media**.
notes.14: Hold two numbers from the study: four Hindi dailies capture 76.45% of national Hindi readership, and two Telugu papers reach 71.13% of that market. Plural nationally and concentrated regionally, so **the regional market is the one to map**. Remember the research dates from 2018 and 2019.
notes.15: Turn the concentration finding into a to-do list. If two papers reach most readers of a language, a story they decline may run nowhere in it. The three 'what practitioners do' lines are your response: **map owners, use more than one outlet and keep owned channels** as a backstop.
notes.16: Follow the money to understand your risk. When a state government is a paper's largest advertiser, criticising its schemes carries a commercial cost. The slide's remedy is practical: brief several outlets and **publish the full study on your own site the same day**. Never offer paid placement for coverage.
notes.17: Treat the percentages as a translation budget. Hindi at 43.63% leads, and six more scheduled languages each hold between roughly 4% and 8%. The action line is the one to copy: **release translations the same day** as the English version, or someone else's summary will frame your work.
notes.18: Be wary of judging a launch by two English dailies. They matter for national circles, but the district health staff and families you want to reach read the language press. Budget for translation and a spokesperson in each language, because **a translated two-page summary** lands where programme decisions are made.
notes.19: Treat each country as its own risk map. The slide gives one legal fact per country and warns that a strategy working in Kathmandu may expose a partner in Dhaka or Lahore. Ask local partners what the law allows and **let them decide whether to be quoted**.
notes.21: Use these figures to see why the public broadcaster still matters: Akashvani's transmitters cover 98% of the population, and DD FreeDish needs no monthly subscription. When your audience pays for neither cable nor data, **Akashvani and FreeDish are the route** that reaches them.
notes.22: Check the news rule before you pitch a station. Private FM and community stations cannot originate news, while Akashvani's regional news units can. For a study launch, **go to Akashvani for news**, use FM for announcements and community radio for talk shows and phone-ins.
notes.23: Read the table as eligibility plus limits. Applicants need three years of community service, at least 50% locally generated content and a 5-10 km range, with advertising capped at 12 minutes an hour. The row that catches NGOs is the last: **only Akashvani news**, unedited or faithfully translated.
notes.24: Notice that two official sources disagree, 528 against 564, and the slide offers three possible reasons. Copy the habit at the foot: **name the source and the date**, and if two sources disagree, say which you used and why. Readers trust a communicator who shows the seams.
notes.25: Use the do and avoid lists as a partnership checklist. These stations are small, local and easily overloaded, so bring content their community wants, local speakers and a production budget. A press release read aloud is the usual failure, so **offer a programme idea in their language**.
notes.26: Read SITE and Kheda as two stages of one argument. SITE tested centrally produced television at scale, and Kheda shaped content around one district's problems. The last line points to section 7: **a shift from broadcasting messages to people towards producing them with people**.
notes.27: Use the table to see how households receive television, then read the sentence at the foot. Of the 917 permitted channels, 908 are available for downlinking. Pay DTH subscribers fell from 50.99 to 49.05 million in one quarter. Free satellite and public broadcasting reach households that **neither pay for television nor use much mobile data**.
notes.29: Read these figures with the sample in mind. The Reuters sample is mostly English-speaking and online, so it describes urban, connected audiences, who include most policy-makers. The practical point: **a trusted creator's ten-minute explainer** may reach more of this audience than a newspaper article.
notes.30: Trust in news is 39%, eighteenth of 48 markets and down four points, so the outlet you choose lends its reputation to your work. The slide's advice is concrete: aim for outlets trusted across political lines, **publish your data and method** and correct errors in the open.
notes.31: The difference sits in the Correction row. In a public feed a correction can be attached to the claim, while in a chat it must travel the same chain. Design for that. A short local-language voice note or image card from **a source the group already trusts** is the format that travels.
notes.32: Note the method before you cite the finding: about 275 users in four states, reached through 65 interviews, 16 focus groups and 10 expert interviews. Describe it as **qualitative fieldwork in four states** in 2019, since the sample was never national.
notes.33: Remember the finding that overturns a common assumption: prejudice and ideology, more than digital illiteracy, drove the sharing, and sharing followed caste, religion and gender. So digital literacy training alone will not stop hateful misinformation. The authors' alternative is **critical media literacy** built on constitutional values and human rights.
notes.34: Use the four-step loop as an incident procedure and practise it before you need it. The correction is short and leads with the accurate fact, a source and what people can do. **Keep the false claim out of the headline and image**, and answer in the language the rumour travels in.
notes.35: Plan for darkness. The slide counts at least 313 shutdowns in 52 countries in 2025, 195 of them in 11 Asia-Pacific countries. Triggers include protests, exams and elections, so **keep an offline route for every critical message**: radio, printed material or frontline workers.
notes.37: Read both rank and category. India is 157th of 180 with a score of 31.96, in RSF's 'very serious' band, and fell six places. Nepal at 87 is the regional outlier. For a regional campaign, **use the category as your risk signal** and the rank for the direction of travel.
notes.38: Know what the number is made of before you quote it. Five contextual indicators feed the score, and part of it rests on expert perceptions, so a few points can move a country many places. Always name the edition and method, and **treat small rank moves with caution**.
notes.39: Learn the logic in one line: the Constitution has no separate press clause, so the press is free because speech is free under Article 19(1)(a). Romesh Thappar (1950) is the case to remember, where the Court **struck down a ban on a weekly's circulation** because the state's grounds were not then covered by Article 19(2).
notes.40: Memorise the eight grounds as a checklist for any law that limits what you publish. The slide's three-part test is the useful bit: a restriction must fall within a ground, link closely to it and be proportionate. Anuradha Bhasin applied **proportionality to internet suspensions**.
notes.41: Use Shreya Singhal as the model of a successful challenge. Section 66A fell entirely, while the blocking power in s69A was upheld and s79 was read down. So **an online-speech law can fall in part and stand in part**, and you need to read each section.
notes.42: Keep the four directions in mind: publish the orders, no indefinite suspension, temporary only, and proportionate and reviewable. For a field programme, the practical step is on the slide: **ask for the order**, then rely on its stated duration and reasons in any advocacy or challenge.
notes.43: Read this slide as a warning about cost. Criminal defamation survived challenge in 2016, the offence now sits in BNS s356, and a complaint can be filed in a court far from your office. The slide names the real penalty: **legal cost and time**. Check facts and wording every time.
notes.44: Duty of care starts the moment a journalist uses your contacts. Local reporters and stringers covering land, mining, sand, elections or caste violence face the most danger. Agree in advance how sources will be described, and **never name a source or village without informed agreement**.
notes.46: Use the table as an index to the legal slides. Each row pairs a risk with a typical trigger, and most triggers are everyday: a village name in a case study, a photograph you did not commission, a campaign-style message near polls. Find the row that matches **your next publication**.
notes.47: Read the definition for three things: words or pictures, intent or reason to believe harm, and the excepted cases. Companies and associations can be defamed, so naming a contractor is within reach. The complaint rule explains why cases are filed far away: **the complainant chooses the court**.
notes.48: Use the five exceptions as a pre-publication method. Keep notes, data and drafts so you can show truth and good faith. The slide's rule of thumb is a good habit: describe what the data show, **attribute every allegation** and print the response of the party criticised.
notes.49: Find out whether Part III applies to you before worrying about it. It covers online publishers of news and current affairs content, with three levels of grievance handling, and key rules were stayed in 2021. An NGO website is usually not a news publisher, but **a regular news video channel might be**.
notes.50: Follow the timeline as a lesson in how fast the law moves. A rule amended in 2023 split the High Court, was stayed in the Supreme Court, was struck down by majority in September 2024, and was on appeal in 2026. So **always check the current status** before relying on a provision.
notes.51: Use this table as an editorial checklist for your own publications. Norm 9 asks for prompt corrections, 41 for the reply of anyone criticised, and 42 and 39(b) protect victims and limit suicide reporting. Norm 34 asks you to check imputations with the person concerned and **carry their version**.
notes.52: Two rule sets surprise communicators: the programme code for anything transmitted on cable, which includes a public service spot, and election-period restrictions. The practical rule is to pause campaign-style messaging near polling and **check the Election Commission's current instructions** for the election in question.
notes.53: Remember the default for commissioned photographs: if you pay, you usually own the copyright unless the contract says otherwise. Write the contract anyway, covering credit, reuse and consent. Fair dealing lets you quote to review or report, and it **does not cover** a stock image in a brochure.
notes.54: Read the table by date. Definitions and the Board are in force, s6(9) and s27(1)(d) follow on 13 November 2026, and duties and penalties on 13 May 2027. The advice is to start now: treat **photographs, testimonies, mailing lists and WhatsApp groups as personal data** and record consent.
notes.56: Treat Lerner and Schramm as the starting assumption: more media exposure leads to new attitudes and then new behaviour, with information flowing from experts to the public. SITE was designed in that spirit. Keep this as the baseline that **makes the later critiques easy to follow**.
notes.57: The four-step sequence is simplified, so use it as a memory aid. What still holds is that neighbours and trusted local adopters move practice more than a radio advertisement. What the model missed was people who lacked land, credit, time or power, whom it **labelled laggards**.
notes.58: Use the five criticisms as a checklist on any campaign plan: top-down, deficit view, blind to structure, pro-innovation bias and media-centric. The critique carried weight because **Rogers had popularised diffusion himself**. Pick one of the five and test your own plan against it.
notes.59: Freire's contrast is the one to take away. In the banking model experts deposit a message and success is repetition. In the dialogic model communities define the problem and success includes acting on their own analysis, **even against the programme**. Decide which model your next campaign uses.
notes.60: Compare the two columns row by row and place your project on each. Most real programmes combine both, and the slide shows how: a mass campaign tells people a scheme exists, and a participatory process **reveals why they still cannot use it**.
notes.61: Choose your label with care before promising a funder anything. Behaviour change, media advocacy, research communication and community media have different aims and tools, and the last column points to other decks. Avoid promising **behaviour change from what is really media relations**.
notes.62: Use the warning signs as an audit of your own participation. The same few speakers, women and Dalit and Adivasi members who appear only in photographs, uncritical content and decisions taken beforehand all point to token participation. The test at the foot: **could those consulted change the plan?**
notes.64: Plan the products before the study ends. The table names five readers, each needing a different format and length, and the order matters: write the full report first, then the brief, then the release. **Link every shorter document to the longer one** so readers can check.
notes.65: Walk down the six parts as you draft. The inverted pyramid puts the finding first, because journalists decide in seconds whether to read on. Good habits include a named contact who answers the phone, sensibly rounded numbers with a source, and **no jargon such as capacity building**.
notes.66: Compare the two versions and list what the 'after' has that the 'before' lacks: a number, a place, a comparison, a cause and a specific ask. The example is invented, so in your real release **every one of those must be true and checkable**.
notes.67: Use the five-part structure as a drafting frame: hook, argument, evidence, counter-argument, close. Editors want one clear argument for a general reader. Time the piece to a decision such as a budget or a data release, and **disclose any funding** from a party to the debate.
notes.68: Use the reader's six questions as your outline, in the order the reader would ask them. An explainer informs without arguing a position, so it suits organisations that do not want to ask an editor to publish advocacy. The same list works for a video, a radio script or a **WhatsApp card**.
notes.69: Practise the weak and better pair. The weak line is technically derivable but hides the level: 33.3 to 64.3 is a 93% relative rise, and readers will hear '93% are online'. The better line gives level, change and comparison, and uses **percentage points** for the difference.
notes.70: Run your draft through the table: name the people, say what was done, name the bodies, give the numbers, be specific and use the unit readers use. The last row concerns audience: **Indian readers use lakh and crore**, so give the million equivalent in brackets once for international readers.
notes.72: Think like the newsroom. Beat reporters, desks, editors and stringers all touch your story, and a reporter may cover three stories on your release day. Give them a news angle in the first sentence and checkable data, and **build relationships before you need them**.
notes.73: Run your study through the six news values and note which ones it meets. Novelty, impact, proximity, timeliness, conflict and human interest each have a matching move on the slide. A regional editor will ask for **district figures for the paper's circulation area**, so lead with those.
notes.74: Use an embargo only when it buys better coverage, and remember it runs on trust with no legal force. State it with a time zone in the subject line and on every document. The four-step sequence ends by **publishing on your own site at embargo time**.
notes.75: Agree the terms before the interview and assume everything is on the record when unsure. Prepare three messages, each with a fact, plus hard questions and a card of numbers. In the interview, answer the question asked and say **'I don't know, I'll check'** when you don't.
notes.76: Follow the four-step ladder and begin politely: first check whether it is a factual error or a framing you dislike, then write to the reporter with evidence. For your own errors, correct faster than you would expect of others, with **a dated note saying what changed**.
notes.77: Give each account an editor, a policy and a log. The policy covers who posts, photographs with consent on file, response times and personal opinions, and the security list starts with **two-factor authentication** and organisation-owned logins. Post in the languages your audiences use.
notes.78: Offer data in a form journalists can use correctly: a clean dataset with a codebook, design and weights, known limitations, a technical contact and the licence. Repeat the warning to your team: **never share individual-level data** that could identify a respondent, and check small cells.
notes.80: Read the four Dóchas commitments as questions to ask of any image: is it authentic, who shaped the story, was consent informed, and could it harm the contributor? The slide's first lines name the habit to break: **showing poor people as helpless**.
notes.81: Consent has four steps: explain, ask, record, respect. People must understand who will see the image, where and for how long, and be able to refuse without losing a service. **Build a consent log now**, since the DPDP duties begin on 13 May 2027.
notes.82: Treat the statutes as hard limits and UNICEF as the wider ethic. Both laws bar identifying details such as name, address, school and photograph. UNICEF adds that a story must not put the child, siblings or peers at risk, **even when identities are changed**.
notes.83: Learn the remote identification test: could anyone work out who she is? A blurred face with a named village, a husband's name, a school uniform or a distinctive house can identify a survivor. Section 72 and Nipun Saxena bind you in every medium, and **PCI Norm 42 repeats the rule**.
notes.84: Run the checklist on every photograph, video and case study, including those in donor reports. The first list wants yes to all five, and a yes to any item on the stop list means you do not publish. When in doubt, **use an illustration**, since a drawing can tell a survivor's story safely.
notes.85: Map each CERC principle to a sentence you could actually say. Be first with what you know and when you will update, be right about what is not yet known, and express empathy before facts. Keep the six to hand: **first, right, credible, empathy, action, respect**.
notes.86: Agree the timeline and the spokesperson before a crisis. The first two hours go to safety and care, hours two to six to facts, one spokesperson and a holding statement. Never say 'no comment', and for safeguarding incidents **start with a survivor-centred process**.
notes.87: Treat accessibility as a legal duty and a routine. The list is practical: captions, transcripts, Indian Sign Language for key announcements, alt text, readable PDFs, contrast and easy-read versions. For language, **test translations with native speakers** from the community and keep numbers consistent across versions.
notes.89: Climb the ladder from outputs to impact: objectives, inputs, outputs, outtakes, outcomes, impact. Most reports stop at counts of releases and followers. The development-work box is the one to apply: **link communication indicators to the programme's results framework**.
notes.90: Choose a few indicators at each stage and set them before launch. Media monitoring covers only the outputs row, so add downloads and officials' questions for outtakes and short interviews for outcomes. One to remember: **accuracy of coverage is an indicator**, because ten wrong articles are worse than two right ones.
notes.91: Fill this in months before release with programme, research and leadership staff. The example column shows the level of detail to aim for: a decision, named audiences, one sentence per audience, credible messengers, channels, timing, risks and measures. **If a cell is vague, the plan is not ready**.
notes.92: Use the table as a gate. Where the decision says stop, do not publish until the problem is fixed or a lawyer has advised. For an allegation of wrongdoing, the route is evidence, a request for response and **their reply included**. Keep it beside the checklist on slide 96.
notes.93: Read this setup as a problem statement. An NGO has a finding about missed instalments caused by fixable bank errors. Note that the objective names a department's decision before any outlet appears, and the risks list includes identifying households and misreporting a provisional figure as state-wide.
notes.94: Follow the sequence from private briefing to op-ed. The people who must act hear the findings first, then reporters under embargo, then the public, then districts, then the budget moment. The table adds a **language for each audience**, down to Awadhi and Hindi for women in the districts.
notes.95: Match each problem to its earlier slide: a wrong headline to corrections, a photograph request to consent, a disputed dataset to data stories. Then read the final box: the NGO records the circular as a **contribution** alongside other pressures, without claiming sole credit.
notes.96: Run this list in ten minutes before anything goes out. Its four groups mirror the deck: accuracy, safety and law, reach and accountability. The easy items to forget are labelling provisional figures, asking the person criticised to respond and **linking the full study and data** from every shorter product.
notes.98: Use the ten ideas as a final self-test: can you point to a slide that supports each one? Ideas 1 and 10 bracket the deck, starting from the decision and ending with outcomes and accuracy. The law ideas (5, 6 and 7) are the ones to **recheck against current status** before you publish.
notes.99: Pick your next course by your gap. The slide groups the courses as communication and evidence, and law, ethics and participation. The suggested order is Advocacy Basics, then Data Visualization, then Safeguarding & PSEA, and **read the DPDP course before 13 May 2027**.
